speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, September 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I regret the duty of speaking out against this very bad Bill. However, I am proud to speak up for refugees and for the many thousands of Canadians who have been supporting refugees and have indicated that they will continue to support refugees regardless of whether, as it appears, the Government has changed its policy.
I want to talk about the objectives of the Bill, with which I happen to agree. The objectives as outlined in Clause 1 are:
(a)	to preserve for persons in genuine need of protection access to the procedures for determining refugee claims;
(b)	to control widespread abuse of the procedures for determining refugee claims, particularly in light of organized incidents involving large-scale introduction of persons into Canada to take advantage of those procedures;
(c)	to deter the smuggling of persons into Canada and thereby minimize the exploitation of and risks to persons seeking to come to Canada; and
(d)	to respond to security concerns, including the fulfillment of Canada's obligations in respect of internationally protected persons.
Not only do I agree with those objectives, more important, they are in agreement, in conformity and in harmony with Canada's international undertakings to the United Nations, to the 1951 Convention relating to the status of refugees and the 1967 enlargement of that, which Canada helped to draft.
Let me refer to two sections of the convention for those who have not had the opportunity to study and become familiar with it. There is a general definition of a refugee as a person who, "owing to well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the
country of his nationality and is unable or, owing to such fear, is unwilling to avail himself of the protection of that country". In other words, that is an asylum seeker.
In later articles, Canada undertakes with about 100 other countries several obligations. The most important of them is in Article 33, prohibition of expulsion or return, which internationally is called refoulement. It states that "no contracting state shall expel or return (refouler) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion". In other words, Canada has solemnly contracted not to return a refugee in any manner whatsoever. That means even indirectly, even by sending him to another country that will then send him back to the country where he was persecuted.
Canada, like many other countries, has developed a system for examining people who come to our borders claiming to be refugees to see whether, in fact, they are real refugees. Our obligation is not to return a real refugee. Therefore we cannot exercise that obligation, or we cannot keep that pledge unless we find out whether the person arriving at one of our airports, an American border-crossing point, a sea port or on our shore is a real refugee or not. We must not send him back directly or indirectly to the country where he claims he would be persecuted unless we have found out to our satisfaction and according to our laws that he is not a refugee. That is what is at issue in the Bill. Unfortunately, those good objectives which I read are not carried out in the rest of the clauses of the Bill.
With respect to preserving access, what the Bill does is limit access. With respect to controlling abuse, the Bill falls far short, even after the Government accepted some amendments originally proposed by members of the Opposition. Deterring smugglers was mentioned in the Minister's press statement of last month. He made much of smugglers. Smugglers are mentioned in the objectives yet they are nowhere mentioned in the Bill. There is no adequate provision action to be taken against them. With respect to security, yes, there is action. However, it is not the security of those international persons called refugees who we are obligated to protect but, rather, some other unnamed persons, as well as the security of Canada. Given the evidence, and the lack of evidence, about the dangers, I would say that the Government's provisions greatly over-react on that point.

Immigration Act, 1976
How does this Bill limit the access of people to our refugee determination system? It does so mainly by threatening detention and deportation on suspicion of terrorism. We have been through a clause-by-clause study of the Bill. Therefore, what I will say in general is that there is provision for an enlarged use of the Minister's permit and for a different type of permit use.
Instead of the matter being referred to the security review committee, it is to be referred to the Federal Court, which is not experienced in handling decisions on security matters. Its expertise lies in finding out whether or not a correct procedure has been followed as opposed to examining the contents of a procedure. Therefore refugee claimants may be held, as is stated in the Bill, on suspicion, if the Minister certifies that he has reason to suspect them of being security risks.
They may be detained. They may be deported. They may be denied the opportunity to make a refugee claim, contrary to our obligations under the provisions of the United Nations Convention which states that no matter what, every person must have his refugee claim examined, even if we decide we are not going to let him stay for whatever reason, perhaps for security reasons. If we are going to send him away, then we must send him away in the knowledge that he is a refugee, if that is what has been decided by refugee determination, and we must notify the United Nations. The Government has refused to accept our amendments which would have implemented that part of the Convention which we signed.
Thus it is clear that the Government wants to send out the message, "Refugees not wanted in Canada". The message is that refugees are not wanted unless our overseas officers have selected them and they are economically and politically considered advantageous to Canada as immigrants. Otherwise, refugees are not wanted. The message is, "Do not come to our shores if you are in trouble, we intend to shut the door". That is the message being given to refugees, in violation of the first objective of the Bill.
As a matter of controlling abuse, the Bill could have used the expertise of the Justice Department and the Immigration Department to devise a clause which would punish people who plan to help bogus refugee claimants or bogus immigrants to evade or deceive our immigration authorities. We have had a great deal of trouble in that regard. In fact, the law now provides for that.
The Government has said that there needs to be bigger penalties. It could have simply imposed bigger penalties and allowed for different grades of penalties, depending on whether or not an offence is trivial or major. The Government did not do that.
There is already in the Act, Section 95(a), a provision that every person who comes into Canada at any place other than a port of entry and who fails to report to an immigration officer for examination as required is guilty of an offence and liable to punishment. The Act, Section 95(e), also states that every person who knowingly induces, aids or abets or attempts to
induce, aid or abet any person to contravene any provision of the Act or the regulations is guilty of an offence.
What the Government undertook to do instead was to introduce the proposed Section 95.1 which does something quite different. What the Government undertakes to do is attack people who directly, honestly and openly bring a refugee claimant or advise a refugee claimant of the truth of the Canadian laws, to come to a border point and to offer himself as a refugee claimant to our immigration authorities. That is the right way to do it, as the Minister has said in the House. But that is not what the Bill states. It states:
Every person who knowingly organizes, induces, aids or abets or attempts to organize, aid or abet the coming into Canada of a person who is not in possession of a valid and subsisting visa, passport or travel document where one is required by this Act or the regulations is guilty of an offence-
In other words, what this is saying is that if a person is on the run from the death squads in El Salvador and knows from the experience of his friends that he is not safe in the United States because that country sends back all but 2 per cent or 3 per cent of refugee claimants to El Salvador, where some of these people have been killed, and if that person decides to ask for safety in Canada and any Canadian helps him, then he is liable to two years in jail or a $5,000 fine. That is what the Bill states. The Minister promised he would never do that. Yet we do not know who will be the Minister of Immigration tomorrow. The Minister of Immigration often does not know what his officials are doing until it is too late to do anything about it. Therefore we should not write a law that the Minister says he does not intend to enforce most of the time. Thus the Bill does not do a good job of controlling abuse.
As I have said, it does a smashing job on security. But I think it over-reacts since the RCMP told us that there is no evidence that any of the undocumented people who came in over the past year, about 6,000 of them, were security risks. As the RCMP agreed, security risks do not come in as refugees and ask for their documents to be examined. They come in as expensive visitors with expensive forged documents. Those people are whisked right through, as any expensive visitor happens to be, unless there is some information against him.
Members of the public came to oppose the Bill. They came on as little as one-half a day's notice. There were members of churches, civil liberty associations, the Jewish Congress, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the Coalition for a Just Refugee and Immigration Policy, Rabbi Plaut, who is at this moment in the next building speaking against Bill C-55 and who spoke against this Bill as well, la Coalition de Montreal pour les refugies, and the Canadian Bar Association which asked for amendments.
The Canadian Bar Association asked that the Bill be withdrawn and rewritten, but at the very least that it be amended. The two members of the Opposition who sat on the committee moved quite a number of amendments and then moved still other amendments at report stage earlier this week. 1 will mention just one of the amendments which I moved. It
September 3, 1987

concerns proposed Section 95.1, of which I have spoken. The amendment that I asked for was turned down.
My amendment suggested that the clause be rewritten to say that everyone commits an offence "who knowingly organizes, induces, aids or abets or attempts to organize, induce, aid or abet a person to make a manifestly unfounded or fraudulent refugee claim". That is the situation we are talking about where 3,600 people came from one country and falsely claimed to be refugees, because we know that Jehovah's Witnesses are not persecuted in that country. Those 3,600 people made fraudulent claims, and they were organized to do so. That is what we are talking about, and as it stands that is what this Bill did not address.
I requested an amendment that would make it an offence to assist people to make a manifestly unfounded or fraudulent refugee claim with these larger penalties, and the Government would not rewrite proposed Section 95.1 in that way. The Government added it in as an extra offence. But not in the manner in which it would clarify the law, as suggested by the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) in his speech on second reading, as between hcnest people who are helping refugees and shysters. I quote the actual words of the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni on page 8017 of Hansard. He stated:
We should ensure that those who traffic in illegal refugees for profit are separated from those who deal with refugees out of conscience. I believe that is one of the first amendments we should bring through.
The Hon. Member earlier stated that he "hoped to have the opportunity to sit on the legislative committee, and that this would be one of the first amendments we could make". For whatever reason, the Hon. Member was not put on the legislative committee on that Bill. However, he is on the legislative committee on Bill C-55. But in dealing with the amendments on that Bill, his colleagues did not listen to him.
There is another clause which also limits the country's response to our obligation to refugees. In Clause 8 the Minister is given the power to turn ships away. After we raised the point, as did many others, the Government did make an amendment which somewhat blunts the bad effect of that clause.
It now states that the Minister will have due regard, not only for the safety of the ship and the passengers but for the Convention, and it defines the Convention as the one from which I have read. If that clause is implemented, we will see how it stands up in court, and whether the phrase "having due regard" is a strong enough commitment to not turn away refugee claimants until it is determined whether or not they are refugees, and then not sending them back to the country from which they have fled.
Today we have news of the brief from Renaud Paquet, the National President of the Canada Employment and Immigration Union, to the committee studying Bill C-55 in which he
Immigration Act, 1976
states, among other things, that the members do not believe it is right to ask the immigration employees to do the things that would be required of them under Clause 8; for example, to board the ships, cause them to turn around, and search and seizure.
There is a labour problem with implementing it, which would have been averted if the Government had accepted our amendment to not turn the ship away and let the captain do what he wants with those people that he was paid to transport to Canada. In the south seas that has resulted in thousands of drownings. The ship should not be turned away, it should be escorted into port. The captain should be charged with whatever offences are outlined here or in other law, and a determination made as to whether the passengers are refugee claimants and, if so, if they are real refugees. That would ensure the safety of human lives, and it would be a big deterrent.
We received no response on the most important requests for amendment, therefore, we must ask what the Government is trying to do? The Canadian Ethnocultural Council gave us a clue in the brief that they presented to committee a couple of weeks ago, and a letter sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on August 10, 1987, in which they state:
We are deeply concerned that the result of the information campaign of the Minister and Department of Employment and Immigration has had ruinous effects well beyond C-55.
This was prior to the announcement of Bill C-84. They further state:
Many critics have suggested that the purpose of the campaign was to silence criticism of, and gain support for C-55. If that is the case, the Government may well win the short term battle, but in the process will have done monumental damage to the harmonious race and ethnic relations in Canada.
They further state:
Unlike the hospitable reception by the residents of Charlesville, Nova Scotia, the treatment and internment of the claimants has been mean.
They then list some of the actions that form a pattern. I will not read them all. They point out that reporters were warned not to take pictures in Charlesville. That, Mr. Speaker, is an innovation in Canadian law. They further point out that the arrivals were disallowed contact with the media or community people. They were not informed of their legal rights to see a lawyer. Access was only allowed after Toronto lawyer, Mendel Green, began proceedings for a court injunction.
I am sorry to interrupt the Hon. Member, but perhaps he could bring his remarks to a conclusion as his time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask for unanimous consent for a further five minutes.
Is it the consent of the House to allow the Hon. Member five minutes longer?

Agreed.

This list should be listened to. It is from the Canadian Ethnocultural Council. They also point out that when processing of the claimants began, the first and most controversial case, Mr. Amrik Dhinsa, a person earlier deported, was brought forward and made public. This smacked of the most blatant attempt at creating negative reaction.
When processing of claims began media were disallowed, in a further attempt to control information, and again court proceedings became necessary to gain access. A confidential report of the Task Force on Security and Enforcement of the Department, suggesting problems in recruiting clearance of immigrants for security, was leaked to several papers.
Information of another Sikh in a totally different case, dating back several months, which was received confidentially, was leaked by unidentified sources to The Globe and Mail. Other false information on the 174 claimants was leaked to Maclean's Magazine to the effect that 33 claimants had criminal records. The information has subsequently been proved to be false.
Throughout the time the 174 individuals were not called refugee claimants, but rather illegal aliens, illegal immigrants, migrants, Asians, Sikhs, and East Indians.
At the end of July, rumours persisted that another refugee carrying ship was coming to Canada and the Canadian navy, air force, and coast guard were dispatched, giving the image of an apprehended invasion. Hysteria was climaxed.
The Ethnocultural Council has made its point very well, that there was a campaign by the Government to misrepresent what was going on by wild exaggeration. The effect of that was to produce public hysteria which would force passage of this Bill.
One unfortunate effect of the Bill when it is put into law will be what was noted in yesterday's Globe and Mail and Citizen, that now our immigration officers in Europe are jammed with people who are seeking papers-people whose papers are considered false-airlines seeking information about possibly false visas, or officials who complain that they cannot do their regular work because of all the paper work they are asked to do now that Canada is busy shutting out every refugee claimant who does not have a visa to Canada.
The Bill will not only fail in its stated purposes, but it will help to further disrupt the immigration service of Canada. It is very unfortunate that the Government has taken such a hardnosed line on it. I hope that Parliament will have the Government reconsider.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), for his comments. I would like to ask him a question about the process of developing law which will be applied selectively.
The Minister has said that he will not be prosecuting churches or other agencies which are involved in helping genuine refugees, that the intent of the law is to focus on people who are engaged in wrongful activities, in bringing refugee claimants into Canada under false pretences. However, the law still targets church workers and workers with refugee aid societies. The Minister may say that they will not be prosecuted, but the law is still there.
Could my colleague expand on the concept of developing law which has blanket coverage but, according to the Minister, will be applied very selectively? What are the implications of that for the rule of law in a country like Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it was pointed out by some officials that the decision to prosecute under certain laws is left to a senior official, such as an attorney general or a Minister, in order to avoid cases of mistake. That usually happens in very sensitive or politically related offences which are very difficult to define.
With regard to the immigration matter, the Minister seems to be terrified by the thought of a loophole. We now have loopholes through which elephants could march, but the Minister seems to be terrified of the slightest loophole, period.
The Minister and the Conservative Members of the committee would not make any attempt to make enquiries from legal experts in order to define in law the people who organized the Portugal scam, the Turkey scam, the Brazil scam, the Sikh scam, and whatever other scams of which the Department has been aware. They would make no attempt to define those they wish to prosecute. Instead, they defined a whole class of people comprised of thousands and thousands of Canadians and said that the Minister, in the privacy of his office, will decide which few of those he will prosecute.
Everyone who spoke to the committee, including the Civil Liberties Union and a professor of constitutional law from the University of Toronto, said that it was upside down to write a law to catch thousands when you only want to catch half a dozen. It is a bad precedent for Canadian law that a person cannot read the law to find out what is legal or illegal but will have to guess what the Minister would do in a particular case. That is not the rule of law in a democracy.

Mr. Speaker, we were graced until a few minutes ago with the presence of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), who finally decided that it was time to show up and defend his Bill. I see that he is now hiding behind the curtains; I am glad that he can hear me. He came into the House yesterday and delivered a 10-minute speech from a well prepared text. He then disappeared again without taking the trouble to defend his own legislation. The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) who usually sits behind him is afraid to get up and say one word about this piece of legislation. I have never seen, in the history of Parliament, such cowardly behaviour by any Minister. This has never happened before. The Minister
September 3, 1987

came into the House for 10 minutes yesterday and informed us of a number of interesting things.
We know what you are.

He told us yesterday that Canada's refugee determination system is under siege. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to cast your memory back to the summer of 1986 when a boatload of people arrived in Newfoundland. The Minister has the nerve to come into the House 13 months later, one year and one month later, and tell us that the system is under siege and this legislation is urgently needed. Where was the Minister during the year and one month since the first boatload arrived?
It is a slow siege.

What nerve he has, to come into the House and make the kind of speeches which he made on second and third reading. He told us that the system is under siege. If that is the case, why did he not act before? He had plenty of time to come forward with a thoughtful piece of legislation which would have the support of all Canadians, rather than being criticized as it has been.
In order to illustrate that criticism and the reputation which this legislation is gaining in our learned community, even before proclaimed, I will quote from Professors Angus and Hathaway in the Globe and Mai\ of August 25. They say:
The problem with Bill C-84 is that it effectively guts this most basic international obligation by allowing the minister, acting alone, to decide that a ship should be forced back to sea without giving those on board a chance to show why they deserve protection.
What do you say to that, Mr. Speaker? Yesterday the Minister said:
-Subclause 103.01 of the Bill empowers the Minister either to order a ship captain to sail into port or to send him back.
Why does the Minister not make a clear-cut decision? Why turn the ship around? Why not allow it to be taken in so that the captain can be fined and those who are benefiting from this trade can be brought to court rather than creating an ambiguous situation? If the Minister and the Government are serious about preventing the arrival of people who are not legitimate refugees, why not go to the root of the problem, bring the ship to port, and prosecute the captain and the owner of the boat? This ambiguous position leaves everyone wondering what the Minister really intends to do.
Professors Angus and Hathaway make the following observation about the Bill. They say:
This Bill C-84, however, would make it impossible to sort out the real refugees from the bogus ones, and thus would put Canada in breach of international law.
What do you say to that, Mr. Speaker?
There are many observations in this article which I must skip over, but I will bring to your attention another one which struck me as being important, coming from learned legal
Immigration Act, 1976
people who certainly cannot be accused of having legal preferences. They say:
-the law may make illegal the work of church and other humanitarian agencies that assist undocumented refugees to apply for status under Canadian law.
Why would we make illegal the work of organizations and individuals who are engaged in humanitarian work?
Professors Angus and Hathaway conclude here that the Canadian Government "has engaged in a form of legislative overkill". In all fairness, the Minister dealt with this matter yesterday. He rejected the notion that people will be prosecuted, that is, the prosecution of churches and humanitarian groups. You can find that on page 8708 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker.
But these are new sections in the Act. They were marked as new in the Bill itself by the department. The Minister cannot get away by saying, "Actually this is not a new measure, it always existed". If they existed, they cannot be new. If they are new, they are there for a purpose, to be invoked, and you as a lawyer, I suppose, appreciate that, Mr. Speaker.
If the Government does not intend to use these clauses, people cannot just rely on a promise, on the verbal reassurance given in committee, "Don't worry, it will not apply to the humanitarian engaged refugee organizations". You know very well that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is here today, but tomorrow it will be someone else who will have a different outlook and who will not be bound by the words of the present Minister.
What kind of business is this on the part of the Government, legislating one way and giving promises in the opposite direction, saying "The law is there, but do not take it seriously because we do not mean it for you." Is that your concept of law, Mr. Speaker? Are you then surprised why we are upset about this measure, why we have such a low respect for the Minister, who is not even here to defend the law on this matter, who is telling us that what is new is not new?
There must be some competence here and some way of sticking to what one really means. If the Minister does not mean what is in the proposed legislation, why not accede and accept the motions that emerged here at report stage and delete the clauses that are so offensive?
The two professors, Angus and Hathaway, went on in their analysis to conclude that:
-Bill C-84 is a misguided and uninformed response to the legitimate concerns of Canadians ... Yes, abuse should be deterred, but this can be done without violating international law, without infringing the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and without making a mockery of Canada's strong commitment to human rights.
This is heavy stuff appearing in a newspaper that is known across the nation. It puts into jeopardy and casts a shadow of doubt on the validity of this Bill. Will it be challenged on constitutional grounds?

September 3, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
At the conference of the Canadian Bar Association last week some of your colleagues, Mr. Speaker, I am told, were talking about the necessity of sending Bill C-84 to the Supreme Court of Canada for a constitutional reference to establish whether the Bill will work. Perhaps this Bill will be in the courts for a long time, thus making void this whole effort of allegedly protecting Canada from boatloads of refugees. What kind of reputation does the Government want to have with this kind of behaviour?
I am profoundly surprised, puzzled and upset, because yesterday the Minister in his speech did not clarify his points at all. He actually gave a set 10 minute speech in which he attempted to reply to days and days of submissions in committee and to days and days of debate here, and he then disappeared behind the curtains.
The Canadian Bar Association suggested that instead of the preamble we have now, it should be amended to read that the Bill is intended to ensure that genuine refugees are protected from removal to a country where their lives and freedom may be threatened. What did the Minister say to that? He ignored it. He did not say a word about it.
The Inter-Church Committee for Refugees came forward and said, determine the refugee status first and then decide the security issues, as it is done at the present time. First establish whether or not a person is a bona fide refugee. I think the vast majority of Canadians would find that sensible, desirable and a much quicker way of doing things. Then decide about security. But what did the Minister say about that? He said nothing. He just gave a short 10 minute speech.
We have already dealt with arresting a boat and escorting it to port to permit prosecution. Again, there is an ambivalent statement by the Minister in yesterday's speech which seems to come halfway at least in that direction. What upset us very much was that the Minister would not draw a distinction between racketeers and humanitarian groups. The Canadian Ethnocultural Council made that point, as did other organizations. Yet that input was ignored by a Government which made it a point in the 1984 election to proclaim that it would listen, consult and govern as a result of consultation and listening.
Here we are not talking of dangerous, radical organizations or extremist movements. We are talking of well established respected groups of Canadians, such as the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, even that august body of radicals to which you belong, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Bar Association, not dangerous, subversive types.
They came forward, but not one of their amendments or suggestions has found its way into Bill C-84 in its final form. What a sham. What a disappointment. What a poor performance, particularly when, as I mentioned to you a moment ago, there is a high degree of danger that this piece of legislation once proclaimed will be challenged in the courts and then the whole process will come to a grinding halt. How would you like
to see that happen to you if you were the Minister of Employment and Immigration, Mr. Speaker? You would not, I am sure, and no one else would, because it would make this bunch of Ministers look like fools for having insisted on proceeding with measures shaky in substance alone.
This is why your colleague, the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), on August 13 when we were debating Bill C-84, raised a signal of warning. He had the courage to do it. As you know, he is the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration. He made three very important points which must be repeated. He said some major changes must be made. It took a lot of courage for him to say that, being a backbencher in the Party in Government. He said:
The changes in the refugee determination process which are proposed in this Bill are such that it would be practically impossible for a great number of legitimate refugees to apply for refugee status.
How do you like that, Mr. Speaker. That did not come from a Member of our Party or of the NDP, but from a Tory backbencher who is the chairman of one of our standing committees. The Member for La Prairie went on to say:
There are, 1 am sure, other rational and appropriate solutions to this problem, solutions that would not have us break an international agreement on refugees and that could not be challenged in court on the basis of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
That was the Hon. Member for La Prairie speaking in the House of Commons on August 13.
He made another observation which I thought was not only dead-on but very sensible. He said:
The best way to put the smugglers out of business is to dry up the demand for their services. The best way to stop the queue-jumping is to shorten the queue. In short, if we want more orderly borders, we need more liberal borders.
I am sure he meant liberal, of course, in the small / sense. He has made good, sensible points. Evidently, they were not taken into account and that is very distressing.
The fact is that one year and one month after the ship landed in Newfoundland we are debating a measure which is called an emergency measure. We have been told that the refugee determination system is under siege. The Government had plenty of time to prepare something in a thoughtful manner in consultation with all those involved in the refugee movement. It had the time to produce something that would get the full support of the House, rather than produce panic legislation. It is panic legislation and that is what makes it so objectionable.
The legislation caters to fear. It caters to the lowest instincts in society. It is not funded on the advice of those who were in this business long before this Minister was appointed and who will be there long after the Minister, who has finally come to the House to hear the music, is gone. This kind of stuff will still be on the books, unless it is stopped in the higher courts.
September 3, 1987

It is legislation by pretending not to legislate. Earlier 1 gave the example of proposed Section 91(1). The Minister said that the Section is not new, yet it is new. Then he said that it is there, but he will not use it. He will not prosecute those who are engaged in refugee work. He will not make criminals of Canadians who have been active in that kind of work for years and years, as have the churches. That is legislation by pretending not to legislate.
It is legislation that is blind to international organizations. That is a matter that the Minister did not have the guts to touch upon even once yesterday. Not once in his 10-minute speech did he deal with Canada's international obligations. That kind of weakling is the kind of guy who does not even have the guts to come to the House to defend his own legislation.
You are as bad as you were when you were a Minister. You are not interesting.
He can raise his voice and make empty noises because he is a bully, but he will not be a bully for long.
I was here for Heap because he's interesting, you're not.

We put forward amendments saying that even though it is bad legislation and we don't like it, we will try it for six months and give it a sunset clause. I felt very uncomfortable with that because the sun will not set on this legislation. However, the sun will set on that Minister and the Government. It will take care of reactionary, backward measures like this.
I shall continue now with my intervention, after the interruption of the Minister. This is legislation by loopholes. It closes the loopholes surrounding those who arrive here on boats but, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), so eloquently put it yesterday afternoon, it allows for the same old process for those who arrive here by air or by land. If your brother, Mr. Speaker, is a refugee who arrives by boat, the boat on which he is travelling is likely to be turned around. However, if you are a potential refugee, Mr. Speaker, and you arrive by air, then you will not be treated the same way as your brother who came here by sea. How do you like that for equality of treatment?
It is also legislation by absenteeism, not on the part of one but on the part of two Ministers who chose to stay away when it got too hot in the kitchen. The poor Parliamentary Secretary was left here to steer this matter through in a rather compassionate and competent way. Perhaps the Government was served better by not having these two strange Ministers in the House to defend it.
In the end, it is legislation by cosmetics. It is smoke-and-mirror legislation which does not go to the root of the problem. It damages Canada's world reputation. It has said no to the thoughtful input of a number of organizations which appeared
Immigration Act, 1976
before the committee, the very same constituency that this Government said it would listen to-
I regret that the Hon. Member's time is up. There is time for questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the comments of the Hon. Member. 1 think we can agree that there has been a consensus across Canada that there have been abuses in the refugee system. This consensus across Canada calls for changes to correct those abuses. The consensus is based on public opinion and on the advice and concern of churches and organizations that are specifically involved in helping refugees.
Certainly Members of all three Parties in the House want to see the abuses of the refugee system corrected. There is no question that that consensus exists in Canada and in this House. Yet the Government chose not to proceed in a moderate, intelligent, deliberate manner to correct the abuses. Instead, it brought in such poorly drafted legislation that there is great concern among church groups and refugee-aid groups. It has certainly aroused the opposition of the two opposition Parties as well as a significant number of members of the Conservative Party, although only one or two have had the courage to speak out.
Given the fact that there is this consensus, why has the Government not proceeded in a more deliberate, rational, intelligent manner to correct the abuse? Why has it brought in such poorly drafted, Draconian legislation?

Mr. Speaker, I wish I had the answer to that question. Usually a Minister who proposes a Bill answers that question, not only out of courtesy but out of a desire to explain why the legislation, no matter what it is, appears before the House. Usually the Minister defends it at report stage and third reading, and extensively so, and submits himself or herself to questions of this kind. It is regrettable and more than just unfortunate that this Minister would not do that.
Evidently, as the Hon. Member just said, there is a consensus across Canada for changes and improvements. The Government has chosen not to proceed in a competent and thoughtful manner. I hope that in the course of debate later today, Members on the government side will come forward with answers to the very thoughtful question put by the Hon. Member, because I am not in a position to give a full and comprehensive answer to it.

On the second aspect, that of the interdicting of ships, we would oppose these provisions because of the commitment we have to the clients we serve.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO ROLE PLAYED BY LABOUR
TRIBUTE TO ROLE PLAYED BY LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, labour in Canada has fought a long and tenacious battle to attain today's work standards. In that battle the working men and women stuck together through thick and thin, often in the face of insurmountable odds, to gain a better life for themselves and their families. In doing so there was often suffering, both mental and physical, deaths, hunger and breakdowns, and at the time many a good man or woman would have been unable to stand these pressures without the support of other workers. It is for those reasons that labour has grown so strong and united over the years.
To appreciate the role that labour plays in the running of our nation, try to imagine a Canada without coal produced by coal miners, steel manufactured by steelworkers, fish caught by fishermen and processed by fish plant workers, food grown by farmers, and taxis driven by taxi drivers. The list goes on. With this thought in mind one can easily appreciate the havoc, mass confusion and total breakdown which would occur if our labour force suddenly disappeared or stopped working. Therefore, let us pay tribute to the contributions of the labour movement both in the past and to come in the future, and focus our appreciation of labour on Labour Day next week.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to salute all those individuals who make us proud to be Canadian. There are many, from national heroes such as Rick Hansen, Terry Fox and Norman Bethune, to our honoured veterans, and those who so bravely fought and died for us, and as well, the many local citizens, those often unsung heroes, who give so much of themselves every day.
One such individual who deserves our special attention is Mr. Gerard Lahaie who this summer was tragically killed on the west island of Montreal when he stopped to help a stranger, a woman, repair a flat tire at the side of the highway. Gerard, said one of his co-workers, died the way he lived, helping someone else. He would have chosen no other way.
I know all Hon. Members, who are often so busy and hurried that they have little time for personal thought and reflection, will join me in saluting Mr. Lahaie and all the other great Canadians of their neighbourhoods. We appreciate their efforts and are proud of what they have done for their community and their country. To Gerard Lahaie and all local heroes, thank you.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fast-track approach to a free trade agreement with the United States is quickly approaching and with it a genuine desire to secure the best deal possible for both countries.
Support for a free trade agreement between Canada and our American neighbour was echoed yesterday by Prime Minister Jacques Santer of Luxembourg who said: "It seems to me, from the purely economic point of view, Canada can only benefit from a free trading system with the U.S. and the rest of the world".
Luxembourg, with a population of only 367,000, has free trade agreements and prospers as a result. It has the highest standard of living in the European Community, the European Community's lowest unemployment rate of 1.3 per cent, and the lowest level of annual inflation at 0.3 per cent.

CRITICISM OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where will the isolationist policies of the NDP end, and on how many international obligations will the NDP turn their backs?
First, Canadians heard the NDP policy that they would pull out of NATO and pull out of NORAD. NATO has been the expression of collective western defence since 1949, a multilateral deterrent that provides a stable framework for the management of superpower relations across Europe and the Atlantic.
As French Prime Minister Jacques Chirac said this week: "Isolationism is not desirable for any country in this era".
This week during the Ontario election, the NDP Leader said that an NDP provincial Government would pay up to 40 per cent more for Canadian-made goods over imports and require hospitals, school boards and libraries to do the same, at substantial public expense.
Recently, another isolationist policy emerged from the well-known NDP strategist, Gerald Caplan. He advocates Canada should withdraw from the Group of Seven industrial nations and presumably would have Canada forfeit its hard-won position as a member of the G-7 Finance Ministers as well.
This fortress or bunker mentality emerging from the collective minds of the NDP leaders needs to be seriously understood by Canadians. The NDP's true international allies are starting to emerge. Yesterday the Soviet news agency Tass accused Chirac of "harsh attacks on Canada's New Democratic Party" and also said he had accused the NDP of "dangerous neutrality".

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege and responsibility to present a petition from a number of Canadians who point out that troubles in many parts of the world cause people to seek safety and asylum in Canada and that Canada in the past has established refugee status determination procedures, that these have broken down under the strain of recent years and that a committee of the House has proposed a new procedure which is quicker and fairer than the one now in place and that this procedure has the support of all Parties in the House as well as a number of organizations. However, the Government put in place procedures which turned refugees away.

Therefore, the petitioners call upon Parliament to bring in legislation which embodies the principle of fair and quick oral hearings before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings, and adequate opportunity to arrive in Canada and make the claim.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD

speechtext:
When debate was interrupted at eleven o'clock the Flon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) had six minutes remaining in his question and comment period. 1 will entertain further questions and comments.
There being none, questions and comments are now terminated. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-84. To begin with I would like to say a word of appreciation to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), for his hard work on this issue in committee as it dealt with Bill C-84, as it is working now on C-55, and for his continuing interest in this entire issue. In the spirit of nonpartisanship, I should also say a word of appreciation for the work done by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi).
Similarly, I would like to have been able to say a word of appreciation for the work that the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) would have done on this Bill had he been permitted by the Government to sit on the committee. As we all know, the Hon. Member was the chairperson of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. Over the past few months, as he became more and more aware of the concerns of refugees and the problem of refugee status determination, he took a very active interest. At the same time he saw the Government going in a direction diametrically opposite to what his committee recommended and to that which is considered to be fair and just to the refugees.
The Government brought us back to deal with this legislation. It is the main item on the agenda. This is what constituted the crisis which justified the Government's calling the House back in August. Some 174 boat people landing off the coast of Nova Scotia constitute a crisis. There is a crisis but it is not in Canada particularly. It is a world crisis. It exists because there are over 13 million refugees around the world as defined by the UN Convention. If we look at other kinds of refugees, including those refugees from famine, ecological disaster, and internal causes, there would be many millions more. It has been pointed out that every day, 365 days a year, for the last 30 years, an average of 700 people have become refugees. Yet we create a crisis because 174 of them waded ashore in Nova Scotia.

September 3, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
I would like to share a few figures with you to give you some idea of the magnitude of the problem. In Central America today there are 1.5 million refugees. There are two million Palestinian refugees in the Middle East. Some of these refugees are second and third generation. Some three million Afghans have fled to Pakistan and Iran since the Russian invasion of 1979. Some two million people were displaced in Vietnam, Kampuchea and Laos over the last 10 years. Between 1980 and 1985, 400,000 people were forced to flee from Uganda. Millions of Africans have been displaced by war, internal oppression, famine and ecological disaster such as the advance of the Sahel. In the tragic split of the India subcontinent of 1947, at the time of the partition, over 14 million Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs were displaced. Some of them moved south into India from Pakistan and others moved the opposite way. This is the magnitude of the problem our world has faced in the last few years.
While we in Canada think we have a crisis, the heaviest impact of this crisis has fallen on Third World countries. There are 25 Third World countries where more than 50,000 unassimilated refugees live in camps. The 20 countries with the highest ratio of refugees to local population are all in the Third World, and those countries have a per capita annual income of less than $700.
Sudan is perhaps a particularly outstanding example of the pressure this puts on a poor country. Sudan is under stress politically, economically and ecologically. It has had to create a special department with more than 1,500 people to look after the more than one million refugees who flooded into Sudan from Chad, Ethiopia and Uganda. In some of its refugee camps in the south the mortality rate is about 285 per 1,000. In a 12-month period 285 refugees out of 1,000 would die. That is the tragic condition of refugees in some parts of our world today. Yet we feel we have a crisis in Canada because of 174 boat people.
In May of 1979 there was a special conference on refugees in Africa. President Nyerere of Tanzania spoke to that and I would like to share some of his words. He was speaking particularly to the African situation, but I think it applies to all of us. He said:
Even if there was not a single new refugee in Africa from this day forward, it is relevant to remember that a refugee stays a refugee for up to 70 years if we do not make provision for his or her integration into our societies. Either we make arrangements whereby refugees can become self-supporting or they have to be fed for a lifetime . . . Refugees have only one thing in common-that they have fled from their country. Even the cause of their flight will be different. It may be persecution, or social upheaval, or war, or it may be famine which causes a disregard of borders. The refugees are usually, but not quite always, without property or means of earning a living.
But apart from the fact of seeking refuge they are as varied as Africa's people are varied. They will be of many ideologies or of none, of many different religions, and many different cultures. They may be nomadic or pastoral, just as they may be agriculturalists or urban workers. They will have different levels of education; they will be different in ambition, and in character.
All refugees are certainly victims, but they do not consequently lose their individual ideas about life and their own purpose. They will include the ambitious, the optimist, the pessimist, the honest hard-working man and the
sly delinquent; the person who will make the best of things, and the man who will grumble about everything. And so on. Generalizations about refugees are very dangerous; all that can safely be said is that they have sought refuge.
He goes on to point out how refugees often create large problems for the countries in which they seek asylum. This is particularly the case for Third World countries. Then he says:
Yet refugees are in no position to consider the problems of the country they flee to.
I suggest we should think about that as we debate this legislation; refugees are not in any position to think of the problems of the country to which they are fleeing because they are so preoccupied with their own desperate struggle for some kind of freedom and dignity.
Nyerere talks about the very slow progress that has been made in dealing with the problems of refugees. Indeed, on a world basis, we have fallen back in the last few years. Speaking of Africa, he asks why this is:
I do not believe it is a result of ill will, but rather that all the governments of Africa are busy and hard-pressed, trying daily to perform the miracle of the five loaves and two fishes. They are subject to many pressures from their people and on behalf of economic interests elsewhere. And there is no countervailing pressure in support of the refugee victims of injustice and oppression. The only pressure is our own awareness of Africa's unity and of our common humanity with our brothers and sisters. It appears that this is not a very strong pressure in comparison with others to which we are subject.
I believe we can apply to our world what he said about the common awareness of Africa's unity. The only countervailing pressure to completely closing all doors to refugees is our awareness of our unity as humankind and our obligations as human beings to our brothers and sisters in our common humanity. The question we must ask, with Nyerere, is whether or not in Canada in 1987 it is enough to keep our doors open.
There has been less funding by the United Nations High Commission for Refugees to deal with long-term solutions for the refugee problems. Indeed, of the funding available to the UNHCR in 1970, 80 per cent was going to long-term solutions. However, as the result of the pressure of immediate problems in 1981, that had fallen from 80 per cent to 20 per cent. Last year it had risen again to 40 per cent, but we are still devoting far too little money to the long-term solution of the refugee problem. We then wonder why it is snowballing onto our doorsteps.
There is an important role for affluent countries in the north, such as Canada, to play in helping Third World countries cope with the refugee problems within their own borders. Instead of doing that, we are shutting the door. We are applying more restrictive measures.
Bill C-84 is supposed to deal with an emergency, but the Bill has been hastily drafted, rushed through committee, and the Government has refused to consider some of the well thought out amendments that were presented by opposition Parties. It has refused to listen to the kinds of interventions that have been made by a wide variety of Canadian organizations that
September 3, 1987

appeared to give their testimony. These organizations included representatives of our churches, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Bar Association, and refugee aid organizations. The Government has refused to listen to these considered, well thought out concerns of people who want to correct the abuses but do not want it to create an unjust situation.
The only conclusion one can reach is that the Government is playing on the fears of Canadians. While the fears are real and there is a concern among Canadians, I do not believe that these fears can be justified by the facts. If the Government was responsible, instead of playing on those fears it would attempt to deal with the situation, seek to allay those fears and explain the real facts about refugees.
Canadians have nothing to fear from the number of refugees who have come into Canada over the last 40 years. In the late 1970s and early 1980s we received some 60,000 boat people from Southeast Asia. They have not destroyed the fabric of Canadian society.
Since the 1940s we have received almost 500,000 refugees. They have made an invaluable contribution to Canadian society. We do not have to fear the contribution that refugees will make.
The attitude that we bring to refugees is one of those issues that will determine what kind of people and society we will be in the future. We can either have a society that is open, multiracial and a model for the kind of world we must create if humankind is going to live and prosper on a globe with very finite resources, or we can react as this legislation seems to suggest and move back to a more closed society that characterized the societies of our ancestors.
In early times it was a trait to be afraid of the people who lived in the next village or community, afraid of people who belonged to a different tribe or spoke with a slightly different dialect. Do we want to move back to that kind of closed society?
We have often thought about the kind of contribution refugees and immigrants from different parts of the world have made to Canadian society. We often emphasize the economic and business contributions, but I would like to think about the contribution these people have made to our level of tolerance and understanding. Perhaps I could use an example from my own ancestry to illustrate this. Some of my ancestors came from Ireland over 100 years ago. Like many other people who came from the old country, I presume they brought their prejudices with them. We know that there was a good deal of prejudice between Protestants and Catholics in the early years in Canada. However, 140 years later, that prejudice is left far behind us in Canada. The very idea of Protestant and Catholic bigotry seems sadly outdated, but when we consider the history of Ireland and the current events there, we see that it is still happening. Canadians cannot understand why.
I suggest that we have moved beyond this kind of prejudice and bigotry because, with so many other people coming to our
Immigration Act, 1976
nation, it just did not make sense for two Irishmen to fight over obscure points of religion.
Today, there are interchurch committees on refugees, consisting of Protestant and Catholic churches that come before the House of Commons to request a more open refugee policy. Even 30 years ago, a United Church moderator would complain that there were too many catholic immigrants coming to Canada. There has been a tremendous change in some of our thinking.
I suggest that we owe that change to the fact that so many people have come to Canada and created a multicultural kind of society. Some people have developed new prejudices, but that is another matter. There is still a fear of the stranger, a kind of latent racism.
I would like to share a poem with you, Mr. Speaker, a poem written at the time of the rise of Hitler by W. H. Auden, the English poet. In the poem we see that all the concerns that we have today for documents, committees, politicians, racism, and the fear that refugees will take away our daily bread were there 40 and 50 years ago. The poem is entitled Refugee Blues. The poem is either a Jewish couple talking to each other or a Jewish parent talking to his or her child. The poem reads:
Say this city has ten million souls,
Some are living in mansions, some are living in holes:
Yet there's no place for us, my dear, yet there's no place for us.
Once we had a country and we thought it fair,
Look at the atlas and you'll find it there:
We cannot go there now, my dear, we cannot go there now.
In the village churchyard there grows an old yew,
Every spring it blossoms anew:
Old passports can't do that, my dear, old passports can't do that.
The consul banged the table and said:
'If you've got no passport you're officially dead':
But we are still alive, my dear, but we are still alive.
Went to a committee; they offered me a chair;
Asked me politely to return next year:
But where shall we go to-day, my dear, but where shall we go to-day?
Came to a public meeting; the speaker got up and said:
Tf we let them in, they will steal our daily bread';
He was talking of you and me, my dear, he was talking of you and me.
Thought I heard the thunder rumbling in the sky;
It was Hitler over Europe, saying: 'They must die';
O we were in his mind, my dear, O we were in his mind.
Saw a poodle in a jacket fastened with a pin,
Saw a door opened and a cat let in:

But they weren't German Jews, my dear, but they weren't
German Jews.
Went down the harbour and stood upon the quay,
Saw the fish swimming as if they were free:
Only ten feet away, my dear, only ten feet away.
Walked through a wood, saw the birds in the trees;
They had no politicians and sang at their ease:
They weren't the human race, my dear, they weren't the human race.
Dreamed I saw a building with a thousand floors,
A thousand windows and a thousand doors;
Not one of them was ours, my dear, not one of them was ours.
Stood on a great plain in the falling snow;
Ten thousand soldiers marched to and fro:
Looking for you and me, my dear, looking for you and me.
The situation is that refugees look to Canada, yet it is a country which is closing its doors to them. They are aware of the pressure that comes upon them from everywhere.
The objectives in the Bill are objectives which we can support. However, the measures which the Bill enshrines do not meet those objectives. Therefore we cannot support those measures, i urge the Government to try to look at this Bill from the perspective of refugees around the world who are in desperate need. I urge the Government to look at the issue from the point of view of an open and honest consideration of what Canada can do, not try to trump up more fears, not try to build upon those fears but let us have a sane, honest, open and fair refugee policy.

Mr. Speaker, in his very thoughtful intervention the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) made a very strong case, revealing how this piece of legislation is based on fear and how it really does not go to the root of the problems that Canadians would like to see solved in an expedited and thoughtful manner.
The comments we have heard in committee, as well as in the debate at report stage, have been varied. However, one thing keeps recurring. It is a criticism that is being leveled at us by international organizations. It has to do with the fact that Canada has subscribed to a number of conventions that deal with refugees and that this piece of legislation, Bill C-84, is one that is likely to infringe upon our international obligations concerning refugees. That is likely to put Canada into the position of being criticized for not keeping our word with respect to these conventions.
These are of course very serious criticisms which were made as recently as a couple of weeks ago by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. I would be interested to hear the Hon. Member's comments on this particular aspect of the legislation as it affects our reputation in the world.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, I think that Canada is not alone in developing this type of restrictive
legislation. What we are doing with this legislation is jumping to the head of the pack. We are right in there with countries such as the United States, which is now shutting its doors to refugees. This legislation must certainly make groups such as the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, which awarded the Nansen Medal to Canada last year for our open door policy to refugees, wonder what impact awarding the medal had. It is like when parents praise a child for doing something good the child feels that it somehow has to compensate by doing something bad. The child does this to show that it is really not as good as what the parents had said it was. Canada was complimented for a good policy toward refugees and we now turn around and show that we are really not as good as what the Nansen Medal would indicate.
I am not a lawyer. I cannot say whether or not this law specifically violates the international covenants. I think that is a question in which the legal fraternity can engage. However, it certainly violates the spirit of those covenants. The spirit of those covenants is that Canada has a fair refugee determination process. That is being broken by this legislation.
The concept of being able to turn boats back, a provision which is contained in this Bill, violates the tradition that Canada had which spoke out against other nations which turned boats back when faced with a much more serious problem than was Canada. I refer to countries such as Malaysia and the Philippines. In those countries there was a steady flow of boat people arriving on their shores. To its credit Canada spoke out against that practice. We said that the boats should not be turned back, that that action put the lives of potential refugees in danger. We are now doing the same thing. Not only are we violating our commitments but we can also be accused of a form of international hypocrisy. We say one thing to Third World countries such as Malaysia and then we do the same thing ourselves.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) has just outlined the difficulty that Canada is placing itself in internationally, in that it appears to be a hypocrite by saying one thing and then changing its policy with regard to refugees. Can the Hon. Member comment on the Bill from the standpoint-not as a lawyer, since he has disclaimed being a lawyer, but from the point of view of a minister of the church? Ministers also tend to learn something about the law and respect for the law. I wonder what his assessment is of the type of Bill that we have before us in Bill C-84. It lays out some very harsh penalties for people who aid and abet human beings who are seeking refuge in our country. How does the Hon. Member square that with the comments and the only defence from government Members when they say that they will blink their eyes at this particular law? What type of signals does that send out to Canadians from the standpoint of obeying and recognizing the law?
September 3, 1987

Certainly, it must be a confusing signal. In the past the Government has urged churches and refugee aid committees to help refugees. Now a law is being passed that makes helping people who have no proper documentation to be accepted as refugees an offence which carries severe penalties. We have encouraged them, and now we are passing a law that states it is illegal.
Then the Minister states, "We are not aiming this law at you, we are trying to get at the agents who are doing this for profit and commercial purposes". What are the people in the churches to think of this whole situation? On the one hand they have been encouraged to be involved in this activity, and now they are told that it is illegal, but not to worry, they will not be prosecuted. It puts the churches in the same category as young people who smoke dope. They never know when the heavy arm of the law will come down on them. It is a law that will be selectively applied. It is a bad law. It should not be accepted by any Government that has any respect for the rule of law in a free and democratic society.

speechtext: The time for questions and comments has expired. Debate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this third reading debate on Bill C-84. Mr. Speaker, I did not have the opportunity to join the debate on second reading nor in the parliamentary committee which examined this issue over the past few weeks. Still I should like to make a few very brief comments in the House today-I do not intend to prolong the study of this legislative measure even though I do not agree with it-to let Hon. Members know that I am against the Bill as presented by the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I do not support the Bill, but nobody should conclude that I condone the activities of people who arrive here by circumventing the law. You know very well that I have no sympathy for people who break the laws of our country and that, like all other Canadians, I too wish Canada had the legislation required to curb such abuses, as I said a moment ago.

We should all remember that the situation brought to the attention of the Canadian public, largely because of the Tory Government, is not something new. It did not happen one day this summer. Indeed, a boatload of refugees arrived in Canada over one year ago. The Government did nothing. A year later, a second boatload arrives with 174 people from the Indian subcontinent. This time the Government is trying to cling to power desperately; it is right at the bottom of the public opinion totem pole, it is scandal-ridden, and defective in every single way, shape, and form, it has lost the confidence of the Canadian people, and it just happens that the Government
Immigration Act, 1976
decides that this second event is going to be a crisis of large proportion.
The Government failed to tell Canadians that that was not the only day in 1987 when refugees arrived on our shores. In the year 1986, 18,000 people claimed refugee status here. That is 346 people per week. However, 174 show up one day this year and the Government decides, that's it, right now there is a crisis, Parliament must be recalled. It just happens that the Government has this multinational drug Bill it wants to pass as well, but that is not the real reason, of course. It only wants to recall Parliament to deal with this issue, say the Tories across the way.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, being the objective non-partisan person that you are, one can never, ever believe a Tory, because they brought us here under those false pretences. What they really wanted to do was sweeten the pot for the free trade negotiations and pass the objectionable drug Bill. At the same time the Government thought it would use this issue to drum up some support. As the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) eloquently and correctly stated earlier today, the Government was using in every means possible in a desperate attempt to drum up support.
Earlier this summer the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) told us that it was an emergency and Parliament had to be recalled. The Prime Minister in his deep, serious voice, that few of us believe but with which we are all familiar, stated that Parliament had to be recalled quickly, right away. Two weeks later the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) found out that no one had advised the Speaker that Parliament had to be recalled. It slipped their minds. After all, it was only an emergency so one could not think of everything. The Prime Minister and his cronies were busy shining their Gucci shoes and did not have time to think of it. Finally, two weeks later, they advised the Speaker and, of course, Mr. Speaker did agree to recall Parliament within a few days.
The point I am making is that a boatload of refugees arrived a year before, and it is not an emergency. A year later a second boatload arrives, and then it is declared to be an emergency two weeks after the boat arrived, and two weeks later no one tells the Speaker that it was an emergency in order that the Speaker could recall Parliament.
We are supposed to believe that the Government is sincere in its approach? I am sure a few people believe the Government is sincere, but I am not one of them. I do not believe in the things that it does. I do not believe that the Government could decide one day this year that something was an emergency when 346 people per week for the last year have been claiming refugee status. In 1985, 8,000 people claimed refugee status; in 1986, 18,000 people claimed refugee status; in the first five months of 1987, 10,000 claimed refugee status. But it became an emergency in July at the time the Government was in a desperate position, trying to cling to power, at a time when it was in a desperate position trying to salvage its free trade

Immigration Act, 1976
negotiations, and everything else that was going wrong with the Tories.
Parliament was recalled to deal with this legislation. Many people have brought to your attention. Sir, and to the attention of the Canadian public and the House of Commons that the Bill is seriously flawed. The Bill states that we have to punish people who bring in refugees. I could be punished. In the mid-1970s 1 participated in bringing the boat people from South East Asia. I was one of the people who participated in Project 4000 under the leadership of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), who was then the Mayor of Ottawa. At that time as Mayor of Ottawa she directed a very successful project of which I was a member. If I did that today would 1 be a criminal, according to the Tories? That is what the Bill states. What it ought to do is provide punishment for the criminals or the people who have done something wrong. The Bill should provide for the punishment of people who try to bring others to Canada in a fraudulent manner for profit. That is wrong. 1 am the first to say that is wrong, but that does not mean that everyone who participates in helping the underprivileged of this world is a criminal. It is obvious that people who give of their time in an unselfish manner are not criminals.
Finally, one must wonder about the Government. For the second consecutive summer the Government has failed so miserably to accomplish its legislative agenda that it had to recall Parliament. What does that tell you, Mr. Speaker? It tells me, and I am sure you will agree, that the Prime Minister and the Government cannot get their act together. The Government cannot get organized in order to get its legislation through before the summer recess. If the Government had gotten things under control Parliament would not have been recalled for so-called emergency situations two summers in a row.
This was the second attempt this summer to recall Parliament on a so-called emergency. You will recall that the first time the Deputy Prime Minister wanted Parliament recalled to deal with the drug Bill. As you know, he was more or less told by the Speaker to get lost, and that did not work out. A few weeks later the second so-called emergency arose, and this time the Government succeeded in getting Parliament reconvened, the real reason being to deal with the so-called first emergency rather than the second one.

What I mean, Mr. Speaker, is that for the better part of the year the Government has been wasting the time of the House. Among other things, I would draw your attention to the many hours the House spent on capital punishment, an issue which should not have been brought before the House in the first place.
Why?

Because the matter had been settled a decade earlier already, as the Hon. Member opposite would know. The Prime Minister was quite reluctant to revive the death penalty debate, but he had made a commitment, one of his 338 election promises, and he just had to live up to one of them.
